views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the Trump-Xi G20 dinner from a position of strength but with willingness to negotiate. Hold the existing tariff architecture as leverage, signal readiness to delay the Jan 1 List 3 escalation to 25% if China offers substantive concessions on IP protection, forced tech transfer, and market access. Do not preemptively concede; do not announce new tariffs before the meeting.

SUPPORTING RIBAL: The US holds a mild structural advantage (threat_score = -0.25). China is under considerably more economic pressure: Caixin PMI fell to a 14-month low of 50.6 in August, export orders declined for five straight months, the yuan depreciated ~9% vs USD since April, and analysts estimate the trade war shaves 0.5-0.7pp from China's GDP growth (CNBC, TS Lombard). China cannot match US tariffs dollar-for-dollar and has already retaliated on nearly all it can ($110B vs US $250B). The US economy, by contrast, grew 4.1% in Q2 and unemployment remains low.

However, costs for the US are rising and the situation is not without risk. The S&P 500 erased all 2018 gains by Nov 20 and entered correction territory (down ~10% from Sept highs), driven partly by trade-war uncertainty. FAANG stocks are in bear market territory. The List 3 tariffs (Sept 24) are the first to directly hit US consumer goods — 24% of items are consumer products — and economists estimate this could add ~0.5pp to CPI, with the jump to 25% in January amplifying the pain (Pantheon Macroeconomics). GM announced major layoffs the same week. The APEC summit ended without a joint communique for the first time in history, signaling that the US-China rift is now straining multilateral relationships.

Analysts broadly expect only a 'mock deal' or photo op from the G20 dinner (TS Lombard, CNBC Nov 23). The US should aim higher than that. The leverage is real but not unlimited: pushing toward the full $500B+ tariff threat would risk consumer backlash, deeper market declines, and ally fragmentation. The smarter play is to use the Jan 1 escalation deadline as a negotiating wedge — offer to freeze the rate at 10% in exchange for concrete Chinese commitments on IP, tech transfer, and agricultural purchases. This preserves domestic political advantage (tough on China) while avoiding the inflationary and market costs of full escalation.
key_factors: China's economy under significant pressure: PMI at 14-month lows, yuan down 9%, export orders declining 5 straight months
US stock market in correction territory; S&P 500 erased 2018 gains; FAANG stocks in bear market
List 3 tariffs first to directly hit US consumer goods; scheduled jump from 10% to 25% on Jan 1 would amplify consumer pain
G20 dinner (Dec 1) offers a natural negotiating moment with Xi; leverage exists but is not unlimited
APEC failed to produce joint communique for first time ever — multilateral strain from trade dispute
China cannot match US tariffs dollar-for-dollar ($110B retaliated vs $250B imposed by US)
GM layoffs and tech sector weakness creating domestic political pressure

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
Expect a photo opportunity, a 'mock deal' — and temporary market relief from the much-touted meeting between Trump and Xi at the G-20, said Bo Zhuang, TS Lombard.
Caixin PMI came in at 50.6, the weakest since June 2017. Export sales fell for the fifth straight month. 'China's economy is now facing relatively obvious downward pressure.'
The Dow dropped 552 points and the S&P 500 plunged 1.8%, erasing 2018 gains. FAANG stocks all in bear market territory.
24% of the goods hit by the $200B tariffs are consumer goods — first time consumer goods directly hit. Could add 0.5pp to CPI.
Behind Trump's tough talk is a creeping anxiety about the costs of a prolonged trade war on the financial markets and the broader economy. GM layoffs this week rattled Trump.
